claim: In everyday social environments, demands on attentional resources dynamically shift to balance our attention to targets of interest while alerting us to important objects in our surrounds.
source: In everyday social environments, demands on attentional resources dynamically shift to balance our attention to targets of interest while alerting us to important objects in our surrounds.
evidence: This is a general statement about attention in everyday environments, drawing from established scientific understanding of attentional processes.

claim: Salient events in background scenes significantly suppress phase-locking and gamma responses to the attended sequence.
source: Using natural soundscapes as distractors while subjects attend to a controlled rhythmic sound sequence, we find that salient events in background scenes significantly suppress phase-locking and gamma responses to the attended sequence, countering enhancement effects observed for attended targets.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the EEG study showing suppression of neural responses.

claim: The modulation of neural activity by bottom-up attention is graded by degree of salience of ambient events.
source: In line with a hypothesis of limited attentional resources, the modulation of neural activity by bottom-up attention is graded by degree of salience of ambient events.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing differential effects based on salience levels.

claim: Both forms of attention (endogenous and exogenous) engage a common fronto-parietal network at different time lags.
source: The study also provides insights into the interplay between endogenous and exogenous attention during natural soundscapes, with both forms of attention engaging a common fronto-parietal network at different time lags.
evidence: This claim is supported by source localization analysis showing overlapping brain networks.

claim: Cognitive feedback modulates the encoding of sensory cues to improve the signal-to-noise ratio of attended targets relative to irrelevant maskers.
source: Studies of voluntary ('top-down' or endogenous) attention have shown that cognitive feedback modulates the encoding of sensory cues in order to improve the signal-to-noise ratio of attended targets relative to irrelevant maskers or other objects in the environment (Baluch and Itti, 2011; Desimone and Duncan, 1995; Senkowski et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research studies.

claim: Changes to neural encoding due to attention have been reported across all sensory modalities including auditory, visual, olfactory and somatosensory systems.
source: Whether attending to someone's voice amidst a crowd, or spotting that person in a busy street, or even identifying a particular smell among others, changes to neural encoding due to attention have been reported across all sensory modalities including auditory, visual, olfactory and somatosensory systems and appear to operate across multiple neural scales (Corbetta and Shulman, 2002; Zelano et al., 2005; Bauer et al., 2006; Knudsen, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Enhanced neural encoding in sensory cortex of attended features is a hallmark of selective attention.
source: Some of the hallmarks of selective attention are enhanced neural encoding in sensory cortex of attended features and dynamics (e.g. envelope of an attended speaker; Mazziotta et al., 2001) as well as recruitment of dorsal fronto-parietal circuits mediated by boosted gamma oscillatory activity (Fries, 2009; Baluch and Itti, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Recruitment of dorsal fronto-parietal circuits mediated by boosted gamma oscillatory activity is a hallmark of selective attention.
source: Some of the hallmarks of selective attention are enhanced neural encoding in sensory cortex of attended features and dynamics (e.g. envelope of an attended speaker; Mazziotta et al., 2001) as well as recruitment of dorsal fronto-parietal circuits mediated by boosted gamma oscillatory activity (Fries, 2009; Baluch and Itti, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: There is a well established link between perceptual attributes of salience and their influence on attention deployment in visual scenes.
source: There is a well established link between perceptual attributes of salience and their influence on attention deployment in visual scenes (Borji et al., 2013; Treue, 2003; Wolfe and Horowitz, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research in vision.

claim: Studies of visual salience greatly benefited from natural behaviors such as eye gaze which facilitate tracking subjects' attentional focus.
source: Studies of visual salience greatly benefited from natural behaviors such as eye gaze which facilitate tracking subjects' attentional focus and allow the use of rich and naturalistic stimuli including still pictures and videos (Borji, 2015; Carmi and Itti, 2006; Marius 't Hart et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Visual salience engages both subcortical and cortical circuits that balance sensory conspicuity with task-related information.
source: In parallel, exploration of brain networks implicated in visual salience revealed engagement of both subcortical and cortical circuits that balance the sensory conspicuity of a visual scene with more task-related information to shape attentional orienting to salient visual objects (Veale et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Bottom-up attention engages ventral fronto-parietal circuits that orient subjects' focus to salient stimuli outside the spotlight of voluntary attention.
source: Bottom-up attention also engages ventral fronto-parietal circuits that orient subjects' focus to salient stimuli outside the spotlight of voluntary attention (Corbetta and Shulman, 2002; Fox et al., 2006; Asplund et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The study of auditory bottom-up attention has proven more challenging owing to the difficulty of properly defining behavioral metrics that determine when attention is captured by a salient sound.
source: By comparison, the study of auditory bottom-up attention has proven more challenging owing to the difficulty of properly defining behavioral metrics that determine when attention is captured by a salient sound.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field based on established knowledge.

claim: Recent evidence suggests a correlation between stimulus salience and pupil size.
source: Pupilometry has been explored in auditory salience studies with recent evidence suggesting a correlation between stimulus salience and pupil size (Liao et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2014; Zhao et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: A large component of the pupillary response is driven by the sound's loudness and its local context rather than a full account of its perceptual salience.
source: Still, there are various aspects of this correlation that remain ill understood, with some evidence suggesting that a large component of the pupillary response is driven by the sound's loudness and its local context rather than a full account of its perceptual salience (Liao et al., 2017; Huang and Elhilali, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Mismatch negativity (MMN) can be elicited pre-attentively and is modulated by attention and associated with behavioral measures of distraction.
source: An example of such a response is mismatch negativity (MMN) which can be elicited pre-attentively, though this response is modulated by attention and associated with behavioral measures of distraction (Ririe et al., 2017; Näätänen et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Use of natural soundscapes could extend results observed with simpler oddball sequences and shed light on the privileged processing status of social signals.
source: Similar to established results in vision, use of natural soundscapes could not only extend results observed with simpler oddball sequences; but also shed light on the privileged processing status of social signals that reflect attentional capture in everyday life (Doherty et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a hypothesis about what natural soundscapes could reveal, supported by citation.

claim: The collection of natural sounds includes a variety of contents and compositions from everyday situations taken from public databases such as YouTube and Freesound.
source: The collection includes a variety of contents and compositions, and spans samples from everyday situations taken from public databases such as YouTube and Freesound.
evidence: This describes the stimulus materials used in the study.

claim: The stimulus collection covers various settings such as a busy cafeteria, a ballgame at the stadium, a concert in a symphony hall, a dog park, and a protest in the streets.
source: It covers various settings such as a busy cafeteria, a ballgame at the stadium, a concert in a symphony hall, a dog park, and a protest in the streets.
evidence: This describes the stimulus materials used in the study.

claim: Subjects report a higher overall detection accuracy for the easy condition (75.4%) compared to the hard condition (48.2%).
source: As expected, subjects report a higher overall detection accuracy for the easy condition (75.4%) compared to the hard condition (48.2%).
evidence: This is a behavioral result from the experiment.

claim: Target detection is disrupted by presence of a salient event in the ignored background scenes, with detection accuracy dropping significantly up to a second after onset of the salient event.
source: Moreover, target detection (in both easy and hard conditions) is disrupted by presence of a salient event in the ignored background scenes; and detection accuracy drops significantly over a period up to a second after onset of the salient event [drop in detection accuracy; hard task, t(62) = −5.25, p=1.96*10−6; easy task, t(62) = −5.62, p=4.92*10−7].
evidence: This is a behavioral result from the experiment with statistical support.

claim: Salient events attract listeners' attention away from the task at hand and cause a drop in detection accuracy that is proportional to the salience level of background distractors, especially for high and mid salience events.
source: Salient events attract listeners' attention away from the task at hand and cause a drop in detection accuracy that is proportional to the salience level of background distractors; especially for high and mid salience events [hard task - high salience event t(62) = −4.97, p=5.57*10−6; mid salience event t(62) = −3.70, p=4.54*10−4; low salience event t(62) = −0.75, p=0.46; easy task - high salience event t(62) = −4.20, p=8.54*10−5; mid salience event t(62) = −2.29, p=0.025; low salience event t(62) = −1.51, p=0.14].
evidence: This is a behavioral result from the experiment with statistical support.

claim: The attended tone sequence is presented at a regular tempo of 2.6 Hz and induces a strong overall phase-locked response around this frequency.
source: The attended tone sequence is presented at a regular tempo of 2.6 Hz and induces a strong overall phase-locked response around this frequency despite the concurrent presentation of a natural scene in the background.
evidence: This is a neural result from the EEG experiment.

claim: The phase-locked response shows a strong energy at 2.6 Hz, with a left-lateralized fronto-central response.
source: The plot clearly displays a strong energy at 2.6 Hz, with a left-lateralized fronto-central response, consistent with activation of Heschl's gyrus and conforming to prior observations of precise phase-locking to relatively slow rates in core auditory cortex (Lütkenhöner and Steinsträter, 1998; Liégeois-Chauvel et al., 2004; Stropahl et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a neural result from the EEG experiment, supported by Figure 2A and citations to prior research.

claim: Phase-locking near modulated-tone targets shows an increase in 2.6 Hz power relative to the average level.
source: Phase-locking near modulated-tone targets shows an increase in 2.6 Hz power relative to the average level, reflecting an expected increase in neural power induced by top-down attention (Figure 2B-top).
evidence: This is a neural result from the EEG experiment, supported by Figure 2B.

claim: Phase-locked response is notably reduced when tones coincide with salient events in the background.
source: The same phase-locked response is notably reduced when tones coincide with salient events in the background (Figure 2B-bottom - blue curve), indicating diversion of resources away from the attended sequence and potential markers of distraction caused by salient events in the ignored background.
evidence: This is a neural result from the EEG experiment, supported by Figure 2B.

claim: Phase-locking to 2.6 Hz after target tones increases significantly.
source: Figure 2C shows that phase-locking to 2.6 Hz after target tones increases significantly [t(443)=4.65, p=4.43*10−6], whereas it decreases significantly following salient events [t(443)=−5.89, p < 10−7], relative to preceding non-target tones.
evidence: This is a neural result from the EEG experiment with statistical support, shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Phase-locking to 2.6 Hz decreases significantly following salient events.
source: Figure 2C shows that phase-locking to 2.6 Hz after target tones increases significantly [t(443)=4.65, p=4.43*10−6], whereas it decreases significantly following salient events [t(443)=−5.89, p < 10−7], relative to preceding non-target tones.
evidence: This is a neural result from the EEG experiment with statistical support, shown in Figure 2C.

claim: A random sampling of tones away from target tones or salient events does not show any significant variability in phase-locked power.
source: A random sampling of tones away from target tones or salient events does not show any significant variability [t(443)=−0.78, p=0.43, Bayes Factor 0.072] indicating a relatively stable phase-locked power in 'control' segments of the experiment away from task-relevant targets or bottom-up background events (2C, middle bar).
evidence: This is a neural result from the EEG experiment with statistical support, shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The top-down attentional effect due to target tones is significantly different from the inherent variability in phase-locked responses in 'control' segments.
source: Compared to each other, the top-down attentional effect due to target tones is significantly different from the inherent variability in phase-locked responses in 'control' segments [t(886)=3.81, p=1.48*10−4]; while distraction due to salient events induces a decrease in phase-locking that is significantly different from inherent variability in 'control' segments [t(886)=−3.58, p=3.66*10−3].
evidence: This is a neural result from the EEG experiment with statistical support.

claim: Distraction due to salient events induces a decrease in phase-locking that is significantly different from inherent variability in 'control' segments.
source: Compared to each other, the top-down attentional effect due to target tones is significantly different from the inherent variability in phase-locked responses in 'control' segments [t(886)=3.81, p=1.48*10−4]; while distraction due to salient events induces a decrease in phase-locking that is significantly different from inherent variability in 'control' segments [t(886)=−3.58, p=3.66*10−3].
evidence: This is a neural result from the EEG experiment with statistical support.

claim: The salience-induced decrease in phase-locked energy is modulated in strength by the level of salience of background events.
source: Interestingly, this salience-induced decrease is modulated in strength by the level of salience of background events.
evidence: This is a neural result from the EEG experiment.

claim: The decrease in phase-locked energy is strongest for events with a higher level of salience.
source: The decrease in phase-locked energy is strongest for events with a higher level of salience [t(443)=−3.78, p=1.8*10−4].
evidence: This is a neural result from the EEG experiment with statistical support, shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The decrease in phase-locked energy is significant for events with mid-level salience.
source: It is also significant for events with mid-level salience [t(443)=−2.57, p=0.01], but marginally reduced though not significant for events with the lowest salience [t(359)=1.33, p=0.20, Bayes Factor BF 0.14] (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a neural result from the EEG experiment with statistical support, shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The decrease in phase-locked energy is not significant for events with the lowest salience.
source: It is also significant for events with mid-level salience [t(443)=−2.57, p=0.01], but marginally reduced though not significant for events with the lowest salience [t(359)=1.33, p=0.20, Bayes Factor BF 0.14] (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a neural result from the EEG experiment with statistical support, shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Phase-locking to 2.6 Hz is still significantly reduced relative to non-event control moments when excluding salient events with the highest loudness.
source: This analysis confirms that phase-locking to 2.6 Hz is still significantly reduced relative to non-event control moments [t(443)=−3.88, p < 10−3].
evidence: This is a control analysis from the EEG experiment with statistical support.

claim: Excluding the loudest 25% events by energy in one ERB around the tone frequency still yields a significant reduction in tone-locking.
source: Excluding the loudest 25% events by this measure still yields a significant reduction in tone-locking [t(443)=−4.93, p=1.17*10−6].
evidence: This is a control analysis from the EEG experiment with statistical support.

claim: Salient events share the same global acoustic attributes as non-salient moments in the ambient background across a wide range of features.
source: A Bhattacharyya coefficient -BC- (Kailath, 1967) reveals that salient events share the same global acoustic attributes as non-salient moments in the ambient background across a wide range of features (BC for loudness 0.9655, brightness 0.9851, pitch 0.9867, harmonicity .9775 and scale 0.9868).
evidence: This is an acoustic analysis of the stimuli with quantitative measures.

claim: The significant drop in phase locking is maintained when events are split by strength of low-level acoustic features such as harmonicity or brightness.
source: Morever, the significant drop in phase locking is maintained when events are split by strength of low-level acoustic features such as harmonicity or brightness [High Harmonicity, t(443) = −3.75, p=1.97*10−4; Low Harmonicity, t(443) = −3.77, p=1.82*10−4; High Brightness, t(443) = −4.18, p=3.51*10−5; Low Brightness, t(443) = −3.26, p=1.21*10−3], further validating that the effect of salience is not solely due to low-level acoustic features.
evidence: This is a control analysis from the EEG experiment with statistical support.

claim: A momentary enhancement in decoding accuracy occurs after high salience events compared to a preceding period.
source: Nonetheless, we note a momentary enhancement in decoding accuracy after high salience events compared to a preceding period [paired t-test, t(102) = 2.18, p=0.03] though no such effects are observed in mid [t(113)=−1.09, p=0.28] and low salience [t(107)=0.24, p=0.81] events (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a neural decoding result from the EEG experiment with statistical support, shown in Figure 3.

claim: No enhancement in decoding accuracy is observed for mid and low salience events.
source: Nonetheless, we note a momentary enhancement in decoding accuracy after high salience events compared to a preceding period [paired t-test, t(102) = 2.18, p=0.03] though no such effects are observed in mid [t(113)=−1.09, p=0.28] and low salience [t(107)=0.24, p=0.81] events (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a neural decoding result from the EEG experiment with statistical support, shown in Figure 3.

claim: A strong increase in Gamma activity occurs after the onset of target tones and spans a broad spectral bandwidth from 40 to 120 Hz.
source: Figure 4A depicts a time-frequency profile of neural energy around modulated target tones (0 on the x-axis denotes the start of the target tone). A strong increase in Gamma activity occurs after the onset of target tones and spans a broad spectral bandwidth from 40 to 120 Hz.
evidence: This is a neural result from the EEG experiment, shown in Figure 4A.

claim: There is a decrease in spectral power post-onset of attended tones nearest salient events which is spectrally broad, though strongest in a high-Gamma range (∼60–120 Hz).
source: Figure 4B shows the same time-frequency profile of neural energy relative to attended tones closest to a salient event. The figure clearly shows a decrease in spectral power post-onset of attended tones nearest salient events which is also spectrally broad, though strongest in a high-Gamma range (∼60–120 Hz).
evidence: This is a neural result from the EEG experiment, shown in Figure 4B.

claim: High-Gamma band energy increases significantly following target tones.
source: Figure 4C quantifies the variations of Gamma energy relative to targets, salient events, and control tones as compared to a preceding time window. High-Gamma band energy increases significantly following target tones [t(443)=11.5, p < 10−7]; while it drops significantly for attended tones near salient events [t(443)=−6.83, p < 10−7].
evidence: This is a neural result from the EEG experiment with statistical support, shown in Figure 4C.

claim: High-Gamma band energy drops significantly for attended tones near salient events.
source: Figure 4C quantifies the variations of Gamma energy relative to targets, salient events, and control tones as compared to a preceding time window. High-Gamma band energy increases significantly following target tones [t(443)=11.5, p < 10−7]; while it drops significantly for attended tones near salient events [t(443)=−6.83, p < 10−7].
evidence: This is a neural result from the EEG experiment with statistical support, shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Control non-event segments show no significant variations in Gamma energy.
source: Control non-event segments show no significant variations in Gamma energy [t(443)=1.5, p=0.13, Bayes factor 0.16] confirming a relatively stable Gamma energy throughout the experimental trials overall.
evidence: This is a neural result from the EEG experiment with statistical support, shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The increase in spectral energy around the Gamma band is significantly different in a direct comparison between target and control tones.
source: The increase in spectral energy around the Gamma band is significantly different in a direct comparison between target and control tones [t(886)=10.3, p < 10−7].
evidence: This is a neural result from the EEG experiment with statistical support.

claim: The decrease in spectral energy around the Gamma band is significantly different when comparing salient events against control tones.
source: Similarly, the decrease in spectral energy around the Gamma band is significantly different when comparing salient events against control tones [t(886)=6.68, p < 10−7].
evidence: This is a neural result from the EEG experiment with statistical support.

claim: The Gamma band energy drop is more prominent for higher salience events.
source: As with the decrease in tone locking, the Gamma band energy drop is more prominent for higher salience events [t(443)=−7.72, p < 10−7], is lower but still significant for mid-level salience events [t(443)=−3.64, p=3.02*10−4], but not significant for low salience events [t(443)=0.84, p=0.40, Bayes Factor 0.076] (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a neural result from the EEG experiment with statistical support, shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The Gamma band energy drop is lower but still significant for mid-level salience events.
source: As with the decrease in tone locking, the Gamma band energy drop is more prominent for higher salience events [t(443)=−7.72, p < 10−7], is lower but still significant for mid-level salience events [t(443)=−3.64, p=3.02*10−4], but not significant for low salience events [t(443)=0.84, p=0.40, Bayes Factor 0.076] (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a neural result from the EEG experiment with statistical support, shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The Gamma band energy drop is not significant for low salience events.
source: As with the decrease in tone locking, the Gamma band energy drop is more prominent for higher salience events [t(443)=−7.72, p < 10−7], is lower but still significant for mid-level salience events [t(443)=−3.64, p=3.02*10−4], but not significant for low salience events [t(443)=0.84, p=0.40, Bayes Factor 0.076] (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a neural result from the EEG experiment with statistical support, shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The three levels of salience strength have significantly different changes in gamma power.
source: A one-way ANOVA shows that the three levels of salience strength have significantly different changes in gamma power [F(1329)=20.79, p=1.29*10−9], with all levels found to be significantly different from each other based on a post-hoc Tukey test.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the EEG experiment.

claim: Targets in scenes with negative signed error show a smaller increase in gamma power than events in scenes with positive signed error.
source: Targets in scenes with negative signed error (suggesting that modulated targets were missed due to lower top-down attentional focus) show a smaller increase in gamma power than events in scenes with positive signed error. This difference is significant based on a two-sample t-test [t(886)=−3.96, p=8.06*10−5].
evidence: This is a neural result from the EEG experiment with statistical support.

claim: Salient events within negative signed error scenes showed significantly higher increase in gamma than those in positive signed error scenes.
source: Conversely, salient events within negative signed error scenes showed significantly higher increase in gamma than those in positive signed error scenes [t(886)=4.32, p=1.74*10−5], suggesting that lower top-down attention indicated higher bottom-up attention, and vice versa.
evidence: This is a neural result from the EEG experiment with statistical support.

claim: A significant correlation between Gamma activity in brain voxels is observed about 1 s after tone onset, with bottom-up attention to salient events engaging these circuits about 0.5 s earlier relative to activation by top-down attention.
source: Figure 5B shows that a significant correlation between Gamma activity in brain voxels is observed about 1 s after tone onset, with bottom-up attention to salient events engaging these circuits about 0.5 s earlier relative to activation by top-down attention.
evidence: This is a result from the sparse canonical correlation analysis, shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Canonical vectors reveal a topography with strong contributions of frontal and parietal brain.
source: These canonical vectors show a stable pattern over time lags of significant correlation and reveal a topography with strong contributions of frontal and parietal brain.
evidence: This is a result from the sparse canonical correlation analysis.

claim: The overlap in bottom-up and top-down brain networks reveals engagement of inferior/middle frontal gyrus (IFG/MFG) as well as the superior parietal lobule (SPL).
source: Figure 5C shows a representative profile of overlapped canonical vectors obtained from SCCA analysis corresponding to the the time lag shown with an asterisk in Figure 5B and reveals the engagement of inferior/middle frontal gyrus (IFG/MFG) as well as the superior parietal lobule (SPL).
evidence: This is a result from the sparse canonical correlation analysis, shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Both Gamma energy and tone-locking yield significant predictions above chance for detecting salient events.
source: Figure 6 shows that classification accuracy for each neural marker, measured by the area under the ROC curve. Both Gamma and tone-locking yield significant predictions above chance [Gamma energy: 68.5% accuracy, t(9) = 4.12, p < 10−3; Tone-locking: 73% accuracy, t(9) = 6.03, p < 10−5].
evidence: This is a result from the neural network classification analysis, shown in Figure 6.

claim: The best classification accuracy is achieved when including both Gamma energy and tone-locking features.
source: Interestingly, the best accuracy is achieved when including both features [79% accuracy, t(9) = 7.20, p < 10−7], alluding to the fact that Gamma-band energy and phase-locking may contribute complementary information regarding the presence of attention-grabbing salient events in the background.
evidence: This is a result from the neural network classification analysis, shown in Figure 6.

claim: Gamma-band energy and phase-locking may contribute complementary information regarding the presence of attention-grabbing salient events in the background.
source: Interestingly, the best accuracy is achieved when including both features [79% accuracy, t(9) = 7.20, p < 10−7], alluding to the fact that Gamma-band energy and phase-locking may contribute complementary information regarding the presence of attention-grabbing salient events in the background.
evidence: This is an inference based on the classification results.

claim: Interaction information across gamma energy and tone-locking features results in greater mutual information using both features than the combination of both measures separately.
source: This measure results in greater mutual information I(F1,F2;S)=0.65 using both gamma energy and tone-locking than the combination of both measures I(F1;S)+I(F2;S)=0.23+0.27, again suggesting a possible complimentary role of both features as biomarkers of salience.
evidence: This is a result from the interaction information analysis.

claim: The current study reinforces the view that profound and dynamic changes to neural responses in both sensory and cognitive networks are induced by bottom-up auditory attention.
source: The current study reinforces the view that profound and dynamic changes to neural responses in both sensory and cognitive networks are induced by bottom-up auditory attention.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the experimental results.

claim: Bottom-up auditory attention effects compete with top-down attention for neural resources, interrupting behavioral and neural encoding of the attended stimulus.
source: It further demonstrates that these effects compete with top-down attention for neural resources, interrupting behavioral and neural encoding of the attended stimulus by engaging neural circuits that reflect the cognitive salience of ambient distractors.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the experimental results.

claim: Modulation of both steady-state phase-locked activity and energy in the high gamma band can accurately identify moments in the neural response coinciding with salient events with an accuracy of up to 79%.
source: Modulation of both steady-state phase-locked activity in response to the attended stream as well as energy in the high gamma band is so profound that it can accurately identify moments in the neural response coinciding with these salient events with an accuracy of up to 79% relative to control -non salient- moments.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the classification results.

claim: The dichotomy in phase-locked activity and gamma oscillations strongly suggests shared limited resources devoted to tracking a sequence of interest.
source: The observed changes in both phase-locked activity as well as gamma oscillations dynamically change in opposing directions based on engagement of voluntary or stimulus-driven attention. This dichotomy strongly suggests shared limited resources devoted to tracking a sequence of interest, resulting in either enhancement or suppression of neural encoding of this attended target as a result of occasional competing objects (Lavie, 2005; Scalf et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results supported by citations.

claim: The push-pull action is strongly modulated by the salience of events in the ambient scene which reflect the dynamic acoustic profile of natural sounds and their higher-level perceptual and semantic representations.
source: This push-pull action is strongly modulated by the salience of events in the ambient scene which not only reflect the dynamic acoustic profile of natural sounds, but also their higher-level perceptual and semantic representations, hence shedding light on dynamic reorienting mechanisms underlying the brain's awareness of its surroundings in everyday social environments (Corbetta et al., 2008; Doherty et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results supported by citations.

claim: Trials with lower errors result in higher enhancement of gamma power of targets and lower suppression by salient events.
source: Further evidence of this push-pull interaction is also observed when accounting for subjects' behavior, where trials with lower errors (suggesting higher attentional focus on the dynamic scene) result in higher enhancement of gamma power of targets and lower suppression by salient events; while trials with higher error (suggesting lower attentional focus) result in lower enhancement of targets and higher suppression by salient events.
evidence: This is a result from the behavioral analysis of the EEG experiment.

claim: Trials with higher error result in lower enhancement of targets and higher suppression by salient events.
source: Further evidence of this push-pull interaction is also observed when accounting for subjects' behavior, where trials with lower errors (suggesting higher attentional focus on the dynamic scene) result in higher enhancement of gamma power of targets and lower suppression by salient events; while trials with higher error (suggesting lower attentional focus) result in lower enhancement of targets and higher suppression by salient events.
evidence: This is a result from the behavioral analysis of the EEG experiment.

claim: Enhancement of phase-locking is accepted as one of the hallmarks of top-down attention.
source: The fidelity of the neural representation of an auditory stimulus can be easily quantified by the power of phase-locked responses to the driving rhythm. Enhancement of this phase-locking is accepted as one of the hallmarks of top-down attention and has been observed using a wide range of stimuli from simple tone sequences (similar to targets employed here) to complex signals (e.g. speech) (Elhilali et al., 2009; Mesgarani and Chang, 2012; Fuglsang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a statement about established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Attentional feedback effectively facilitates selection and tracking of objects of interest and suppression of irrelevant sensory information.
source: By enhancing neural encoding of voluntarily-attended sensory inputs relative to other objects in the scene, attentional feedback effectively facilitates selection and tracking of objects of interest and suppression of irrelevant sensory information (Knudsen, 2007; Shamma and Fritz, 2014).
evidence: This is a statement about established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Diverting attention away from the attended stream suppresses the power of phase-locking relative to a baseline level, tapered by the degree of salience of the distracting event.
source: In the current study, we observe that diverting attention away from the attended stream does in fact suppress the power of phase-locking relative to a baseline level, tapered by the degree of salience of the distracting event (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental results shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: The locus of modulated phase-locked activity is generally consistent with core auditory cortex.
source: The locus of this modulated phase-locked activity is generally consistent with core auditory cortex, though no precise topography can be localized from scalp activity only.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the neural results with a caveat about localization limitations.

claim: Engagement of core sensory cortex in both enhancement and suppression of phase-locked responses concurs with a role of auditory cortex in auditory scene analysis and auditory object formation.
source: Still, engagement of core sensory cortex in both enhancement and suppression of phase-locked responses to the attended sequence concurs with a role of auditory cortex in auditory scene analysis and auditory object formation (Ding and Simon, 2012; Leaver and Rauschecker, 2010).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results supported by citations.

claim: The drop of steady-state following responses due to distractors coincides with a significant increase in the encoding of the background scene near highly-salient events.
source: Moreover, the drop of steady-state following responses due to distractors coincides with a significant increase in the encoding of the background scene near highly-salient events, as reflected in the accuracy of the ambient scene reconstruction (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental results shown in Figure 3.

claim: Neural decoding of ignored scenes results in boosted accuracy at specific moments coinciding with salient events.
source: Still, neural decoding of ignored scenes results in boosted accuracy at specific moments coinciding with salient events.
evidence: This is a summary of the decoding results.

claim: Enhancement of neural decoding suggests that neural resources are being diverted during specific moments due to competition for neural representation between the attended target and the salient background object.
source: Such enhancement suggests that neural resources are indeed being diverted during those specific moments due to competition for neural representation between the attended target and the salient background object.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the decoding results.

claim: Diversion of resources is consistent with load theory which posits that capacity limitations dictate the degree to which otherwise ignored sensory information can divert processing capability.
source: Such diversion of resources is consistent with prior reports supporting load theory which posits that capacity limitations dictate the degree to which otherwise ignored sensory information can divert processing capability within and across modalities (Lavie, 2010; Salmi et al., 2009; Molloy et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results supported by citations to load theory.

claim: There are no global differences between moments deemed attention-grabbing vs. background segments in the JHU DNSS dataset in terms of acoustic features.
source: A comparison of acoustic features throughout the background scene shows that there are no global differences between moments deemed attention-grabbing vs. background segments in the JHU DNSS dataset.
evidence: This is a result from the acoustic analysis of the stimuli.

claim: Salient events were not confined to simply louder moments in the scene.
source: Specifically, salient events were not confined to simply louder moments in the scene.
evidence: This is a result from the acoustic analysis of the stimuli.

claim: What makes certain events salient is not the instantaneous acoustic profile independent of context, but rather a relative change in the scene statistics reflecting acoustic, perceptual and semantic manifestations.
source: As such, what makes certain events salient is not the instantaneous acoustic profile independent of context. Instead, it is often a relative change in the scene statistics reflecting not only acoustic changes but also perceptual and semantic manifestations that normally emerge during everyday social settings.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the acoustic analysis results.

claim: Excluding the loudest salient events still reveals a significant drop of phase-locked activity relative to baseline tones.
source: Moreover, excluding the loudest salient events (using both envelope-level and spectral-based measures) still reveals a significant drop of phase-locked activity relative to baseline tones further confirming that this effect cannot be simply attributed to energetic masking of the attended sequence.
evidence: This is a result from the control analysis.

claim: Grouping salient events based on various low-level acoustic attributes shows no difference in the degree of suppressed phase-locking induced by different sub-groups of events.
source: An additional analysis grouping salient events based on various low-level acoustic attributes (harmonicity, brightness) shows no difference in the degree of suppressed phase-locking induced by different sub-groups of events.
evidence: This is a result from the control analysis.

claim: The significant drop in behavioral accuracy in the attended task confirms the distraction effect likely due to disengagement of attentional focus away from the attended sequence.
source: Finally, the significant drop in behavioral accuracy in the attended task further confirms the distraction effect likely due to disengagement of attentional focus away from the attended sequence.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the behavioral results.

claim: Enhancement of high-frequency gamma has been reported in conjunction with top-down attention in auditory, visual, and somatosensory tasks.
source: Specifically, enhancement of high-frequency gamma has been reported in conjunction with top-down attention in auditory, visual, and somatosensory tasks (Debener et al., 2003; Tallon-Baudry et al., 2005; Bauer et al., 2006; Senkowski et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a statement about established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Enhanced gamma oscillations interface with mnemonic processes, particularly encoding of sensory information in short-term memory.
source: While enhanced gamma oscillations index effective sensory processing due to voluntary attention, they also interface with mnemonic processes, particularly encoding of sensory information in short-term memory (Sederberg et al., 2003; Jensen et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a statement about established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The enhancement of gamma energy extends over a period of a few seconds post target onset, in line with previously reported effects of memory consolidation.
source: Given the demands of the current paradigm to remember the number of modulated targets in the attended sequence, it is not surprising to observe that the enhancement of gamma energy extends over a period of a few seconds post target onset, in line with previously reported effects of memory consolidation (Tallon-Baudry and Bertrand, 1999).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results supported by citation.

claim: Modulation of gamma-band activity is very much tied with task demands, the notion of salience, and how it relates to both the perceptual and cognitive load imposed by the task at hand.
source: Second, the modulation of gamma-band activity is very much tied with task demands, the notion of salience, and how it relates to both the perceptual and cognitive load imposed by the task at hand (Lavie, 2005).
evidence: This is a statement about established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The current paradigm emulates natural listening situations, which reaffirms the privileged status of social distractors previously reported in visual tasks.
source: Importantly, the current paradigm emulates natural listening situations, which reaffirms the privileged status of social distractors previously reported in visual tasks (Doherty et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results supported by citation.

claim: Ririe and colleagues reported reduced Local Field Potential activity (including gamma band energy) during audiovisual distraction in medial prefrontal cortex in freely behaving rats.
source: Ririe and colleagues reported reduced Local Field Potential activity (including gamma band energy) during audiovisual distraction in medial prefrontal cortex in freely behaving rats (Ririe et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a citation to prior research.

claim: Bonnefond et al. used MEG in human listeners and reported reduced gamma for distractors during a memory task.
source: Bonnefond et al. used Magentoencephalography (MEG) in human listeners and reported reduced gamma for distractors during a memory task very much in line with observed effects in the current task (Bonnefond and Jensen, 2013).
evidence: This is a citation to prior research.

claim: Modulation of gamma activity has been ruled out as being associated with novel unexpected stimuli.
source: Moreover, modulation of gamma activity has been ruled out as being associated with novel unexpected stimuli (Debener et al., 2003) and is likely linked to ongoing shifts in attentional focus of listeners throughout the task reflecting the interaction between top-down executive control and sound-driven activity.
evidence: This is a statement supported by citation and inference.

claim: There is strong evidence in the literature dissociating dorsal and ventral networks of bottom-up and top-down attentional engagement, respectively.
source: On the one hand, there is strong evidence in the literature dissociating dorsal and ventral networks of bottom-up and top-down attentional engagement, respectively (Corbetta and Shulman, 2002).
evidence: This is a statement about established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Such networks have been reported across sensory tasks suggesting a supramodel attentional circuitry that interfaces with sensory networks.
source: Such networks have been reported across sensory tasks suggesting a supramodel attentional circuitry that interfaces with sensory networks in guiding selection and tracking of targets of interest while maintaining sensitivity to salient objects in a dynamic scene (Spagna et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a statement about established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: There are overlapping brain regions that underlie top-down as well as bottom-up attentional control particularly centered in the lateral prefrontal cortex.
source: On the other hand, there are overlapping brain regions that underlie top-down as well as bottom-up attentional control particularly centered in the lateral prefrontal cortex, and interface between the two systems to guide behavioral responses that not only account for task-guided goals, but also environmentally-relevant stimuli (Asplund et al., 2010; Corbetta et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a statement about established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The analysis shows that there is a coordinated interaction between bottom-up and top-down networks consistent with other reports of a possible shared circuitry, especially in the auditory modality.
source: Our analysis shows that there is a coordinated interaction between these two networks consistent with other reports of a possible shared circuitry, especially in the auditory modality (Alho et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results supported by citation.

claim: The current study specifically reveals a consistent temporal offset in the activation of the two networks.
source: The current study specifically reveals a consistent temporal offset in the activation of the two networks.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental results.

claim: A possible interpretation of the dynamic interaction could be that signals from bottom-up attentional networks interrupt activity in the top-down network, potentially reorienting the locus of attention.
source: A possible interpretation of this dynamic interaction could be that signals from bottom-up attentional networks interrupt activity in the top-down network, potentially reorienting the locus of attention (Ahveninen et al., 2013; Corbetta et al., 2008; Salmi et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations.

claim: Earlier engagement of overlapped networks of attention by salient events may reflect reduced memory consolidation due to a distraction effect.
source: Two, that earlier engagement of overlapped networks of attention by salient events reflects reduced memory consolidation due to a distraction effect, which is itself tied to diminished sensory encoding of the attended rhythm.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the results.

claim: Canonical correlation analysis attempts to circumvent the limitations of comparisons across source topographies in EEG and leverages multivariate techniques to explore relationships between high-dimensional datasets.
source: This approach attempts to circumvent the limitations of comparisons across source topographies in electroencephalography (EEG) and leverages multivariate techniques to explore relationships between high-dimensional datasets which have been championed with great success in numerous applications including neuroimaging, pharmacological and genomic studies (Parkhomenko et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2015; Bilenko and Gallant, 2016).
evidence: This is a statement about the analytical method supported by citations.

claim: The use of kernel-based regularizations with constraints such as sparsity allows mappings between high-dimensional brain images.
source: While applying CCA directly to very high-dimensional data can be challenging or uninterpretable, the use of kernel-based regularizations with constraints such as sparsity as adopted in the current work allows mappings between high-dimensional brain images (Witten et al., 2009; Gao et al., 2015; Uurtio et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a statement about the analytical method supported by citations.

claim: The permutation-based approach yields an optimal way to define statistical significance of observed correlation effects as well as constraints on optimization parameters.
source: The permutation-based approach yields an optimal way to define statistical significance of observed correlation effects as well as constraints on optimization parameters much in line with cross-validation tests performed in statistical analyses, hence reducing bias by the experimenter in defining parameters (Witten and Tibshirani, 2009; Lin et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a statement about the analytical method supported by citations.

claim: The analysis reveals that areas with statistically significant activations lie in inferior parietal and frontal cortices, particularly inferior and medial temporal gyri as well as the superior parietal lobule.
source: Consistent with previous findings, the analysis does reveal that areas with statistically significant activations lie in inferior parietal and frontal cortices, particularly inferior and medial temporal gyri as well as the superior parietal lobule (Alho et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a summary of the source localization results supported by citation.

claim: The use of a naturalistic experimental paradigm provides a range of nuanced ambient distractions similar to what one experiences in everyday life.
source: In conclusion, the use of a naturalistic experimental paradigm provides a range of nuanced ambient distractions similar to what one experiences in everyday life and demonstrates the dynamic competition for attentional resources between task and socially-relevant stimulus-driven cues.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the study design and findings.

claim: The study demonstrates the dynamic competition for attentional resources between task and socially-relevant stimulus-driven cues.
source: In conclusion, the use of a naturalistic experimental paradigm provides a range of nuanced ambient distractions similar to what one experiences in everyday life and demonstrates the dynamic competition for attentional resources between task and socially-relevant stimulus-driven cues.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the study findings.

claim: The study reveals a steady push-pull competition between bottom-up and top-down systems for limited natural resources and active engagement by listeners.
source: It not only sheds light on profound effects of both top-down and bottom-up attention in continuously shaping brain responses, but it also reveals a steady push-pull competition between these two systems for limited natural resources and active engagement by listeners.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the study findings.

claim: Auditory stimuli consisted of scenes from the JHU DNSS database which includes twenty natural scenes, each roughly two minutes in length.
source: Auditory stimuli consisted of scenes from a previous study of auditory salience in natural scenes (Huang and Elhilali, 2017). This JHU DNSS (Dichotic Natural Salience Soundscapes) database includes twenty natural scenes, each roughly two minutes in length.

source: Salience of events in each scene was measured using a dichotic listening behavioral paradigm (see [Huang and Elhilali, 2017] for full details).
evidence: This describes the method for measuring salience, with citation to prior work.

claim: The proportion of subjects attending to a scene compared to all other scenes was defined as salience.
source: The proportion of subjects attending to a scene compared to all other scenes was defined as salience.

claim: Peaks in the derivative of the salience measure were defined as salient events.
source: Peaks in the derivative of this salience measure were defined as salient events.
evidence: This describes the operational definition of salient events used in the study.
